title: One new server, how many keys move?
hook: Add a fifth server to four. Does it take a fifth of the keys, or reshuffle them all?

knows: a key lands in the bucket given by hash mod size (hash-bucket-pileup)
doesNotKnow: that changing the number of servers by one moves most keys under mod, but about 1/n of them on a ring

misconception: Adding one server to a cache cluster moves only the keys the new server takes over.
objective: The learner can explain that under key mod n, going from 4 to 5 servers moves 16 of 20 keys, while on a ring (each key goes to the next server clockwise) a new server only takes keys from its neighbour, about 1/n of them.

claims.text: Under key mod n, adding E (4 to 5 servers) moved 16 of the 20 keys: only keys 0 to 3 kept their server.
claims.source: Enumeration of k = 0..19 (Demo.tsx owner(); builder's node script, 2026-10-14): k mod 4 = k mod 5 only for k = 0, 1, 2, 3 (both equal k, since k < 4). For 4 <= k < 20 they differ, so 16 keys move. Same as the brief's check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own copy of owner() (scratchpad fc21/ns.mjs): mod scheme moves keys 4-19 (16), keeps 0-3; matches reveal and table.

claims.text: On the ring, adding E moved 4 of the 20 keys, all to E, all from its neighbour A. E's spot was picked to give it an even fifth.
claims.source: Designed layout, not a hash (spec company/design/specs/new-server-moves-few-keys.md): key k sits at k/20 of the circle; A, B, C, D sit at 4.5, 9.5, 14.5, 19.5 (5 keys each); E at 3.5. Next server clockwise: keys 0-3 go from A to E and nothing else changes (Demo.tsx owner(); builder's node script, 2026-10-14). The position of E was chosen to show one even share; a hashed position could give E anything from 0 to 15 keys. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own copy of owner() with RING_POS: ring moves keys 0-3, all A->E, nothing else; E ends with 4 = 20/5 (A keeps 1, B-D 5 each). Designed layout is disclosed in the reveal ('E's spot was picked').

claims.text: On a ring a key belongs to the next server clockwise, so a new server only takes keys from the one after it.
claims.source: Inserting a server at position p changes the owner only of keys whose next server clockwise is now p: exactly the keys between p and the previous server, which belonged to the next server after p. All other keys still meet the same server first. Karger et al. 1997 (c6). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Derivation re-checked; holds for any insertion point (only keys between the new point and its predecessor change owner, all from the successor).

claims.text: A formula like key mod n reassigns nearly every key when n changes.
claims.source: If k mod n = k mod (n + 1) = r, then r < n and, since n and n + 1 are coprime, k leaves remainder r on division by n(n + 1) (Chinese remainder theorem). So over a block of n(n + 1) consecutive keys, the two residues agree for exactly n keys (k = 0..n-1 of each block), so a fraction 1/(n + 1) stays and n/(n + 1) moves (80% for 4 to 5). Checked by enumeration for n = 4 in c1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): CRT argument re-checked; enumeration n = 2..9 over 7 blocks gives exactly 1/(n+1) kept each time.

claims.text: With hashed spots, 1,000 per server, and 20,000 keys, about 20% moved, all to E: about 1/n.
claims.source: Builder's node script (2026-10-14): 32-bit FNV-1a, servers A-D then A-E, 1,000 ring points per server named '<server>#<i>', keys 'key-<k>' for k = 0..19,999, next point clockwise. 20.4% moved, all to E. The result depends on the naming: '<server>-<i>' and '<k>' gave 18.3%; the brief's own script gave 19.6% (cm-cs-algorithms, not re-run by the builder). With 100 points per server the builder got 22.7%; the ideal is 1/5 = 20%. The stage does not hash. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Re-implemented 32-bit FNV-1a ring: 1,000 points '<s>#<i>', keys 'key-<k>' -> 20.415% moved, all to E; '-' and bare keys -> 18.28%; 100 points -> 22.74%. All match the builder; 'about 20%' fair.

claims.text: This is consistent hashing (Karger and others, 1997).
claims.source: D. Karger, E. Lehman, T. Leighton, R. Panigrahy, M. Levine, D. Lewin, 'Consistent hashing and random trees: distributed caching protocols for relieving hot spots on the World Wide Web', Proc. 29th ACM STOC, 1997, pp. 654-663. Builder has not opened the paper in this session. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Paper not opened (cs.brown.edu, Wikipedia blocked). Title, authors, STOC '97 pp. 654-663 and that the paper introduced the term 'consistent hashing' corroborated by web-search results (Wikipedia 'Consistent hashing' snippet, course mirrors of the STOC PDF).

recall.question: A cache spreads keys over 9 servers. A 10th server joins. Which scheme moves only about a tenth of the keys?
options: Server = key mod n, with n going from 9 to 10
A ring where each key goes to the next server clockwise
Both move about the same share
recall.why: On the ring the new server only takes the keys just before it, from its neighbour: about 1/10 of them. Under mod n, nearly every key's remainder changes when n does.
